newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen sees no basis for SCI deal.
newsitem.headline: Loewen sees no basis for SCI deal.

text.p: Loewen Group Inc said on Wednesday it could see no sound rationale for a takeover by Service Corp International and it would not feel under more pressure to consider a bid even if SCI raised its offer to US$50 to US$52 a share.
Loewen's board on Tuesday rejected a US$43 a share offer from Houston-based SCI, a rival funeral service company.

Chief executive Ray Loewen, asked on a media conference call whether Loewen's board would feel greater pressure to consider SCI's bid if it were raised to US$50-52 a share, replied that "$50-$52 would not put any pressure on me."
Loewen said his company's growth prospects were superior to SCI's, that it had dramatically "out-hustled" SCI in making acquisitions and that the companies' cultures were too different.
"I can't see any intellectual reason or rationale how the two could come together," Loewen said. "...I do not see any rational reason how they could ever acquire our company."

Loewen said the company's recent deal to acquire the Rose Hills cemetery in Los Angeles would be immediately accretive to earnings, adding US$6.6 million to net earnings in the first year and increasing by more than US$1 million a year.

Loewen said the return on investment when the company exercises its option in four years on Rose Hills would exceed 15 percent. The total price, including buying out investment bank Blackstone Group, Loewen equity and all debt, is about US$294 million, he said.

He forecast that Loewen's revenues this year would exceed US$900 million and would increase by about US$300 million annually. "We're going to be growing by about US$300 million in revenue a year," Loewen said.
He also said the company agrees with forecasts it is on track for earnings per share growth of about 28 percent.
Loewen's strengths "make it almost impossible for Service Corp to give us a bid that is worth us even thinking about without it being dilutive to Service Corp" earnings, he said.

He said he did not think Service Corp, whose current offer consists of stock, could bid without and still make the deal work. Loewen said shareholders had been supportive of the board's position and he heard not heard from any dissenting shareholders.
He said Service Corp next could try to launch a "very, very vicious" short-selling attack on Loewen stock and seek to divide the Loewen board.
Loewen said Service Corp would face "at least a dozen" legal and other hurdles in mounting a hostile bid but he declined to give details.
